name: Colin Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won’t be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on nights, mostly, on an elderly care ward at Harlow Bridge District Hospital, which is the only hospital within an hour of here. I come in at half seven, take handover, and then it's 14 patients between me and a healthcare assistant: meds round, turning people every two hours, checking blood sugars, calming whoever's woken up confused. Around 3am there's always someone trying to climb out of bed or pull their drip out. I get home to the flat above the bakery on Mill Street just as the smell of bread starts coming up through the floor.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the old folks, honestly. You get a lady at 4am who can't sleep and tells you about dancing in the 1960s, and that's the best part of the job. What wears me out is the money and the screens. I'm on the lower end of the pay band, my partner Tom works at the garden centre, and the night allowance is what covers our rent. Now management wants to merge our ward with the one upstairs, and if I get moved to days I lose that allowance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out as it's written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype. That's what I've been saying since they put the new tablets on the ward. Fine, I can picture that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say "told you so", loudly, in the staff room. Half the stuff they sold us as smart is just a slower way of doing the paperwork. I'd probably post something sarcastic in the union group chat about all the money spent on gadgets while we're short of nurses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI flopping doesn't fix anything for me. AI was meant to change everything, and on my ward it changed the font on the drug chart. My rent still went up. The real threat was always the ward merger and the night allowance, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my nights and keep my head down. I'd go to every consultation meeting about the merger and get the union rep, Gwen, to come with me. Tom and I would cut the takeaway on Fridays and cancel the streaming we don't watch, because if I go to days we're short about 300 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. A bit smug that the hype didn't land, but smug doesn't pay the rent. There's a knot in my stomach every time an email from the ward manager comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the merger goes through and you're moved to days, which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably. We'd sell it and I'd get the bus, which means leaving an hour early for a 12-hour shift. Tom would say we should move in with his mum, and I'd rather sleep in the sluice room than do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI flopping fixes nothing. Is there any part of the routine stuff it does take over that you'd be glad of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the stock ordering, if it actually worked. Right now I spend twenty minutes a night counting dressings because the system never knows what we've got. If a computer did that properly I'd give it a grudging nod, but I'm not holding my breath.

say: I'd tell everyone in the **staff room** that the tablets were never as smart as promised.
I'd post something **sarcastic** in the union chat about gadgets bought while we're short of nurses.
think: AI flopping changes **nothing** for me, because my real problem is low pay and rising rent.
The **ward merger** is the actual threat, because it could take away my night allowance.
do: Keep working **nights** and keep my head down while the merger talks go on.
Bring the **union rep** to every consultation meeting about merging the two elderly care wards.
Cut **takeaways and streaming** now, since moving to days would leave us about 300 short a month.
feel: **Tired** and a bit smug that the hype failed, but smugness doesn't pay rent.
A **knot** in his stomach whenever an email arrives from the ward manager.
S0.quote: AI was meant to change everything, and on my ward it changed the font on the drug chart. My rent still went up.
fieldNote: His worry in this picture has **nothing to do** with AI; it's the ward merger and losing night pay.
He'd sell the car before **moving in** with his partner's mother, which says a lot about his pride.
Grudging respect for AI only if it fixed **stock counting**, a small, specific annoyance.

steps.text: Keep working night shifts on the elderly care ward
Take the union rep to every ward merger meeting
Cancel the streaming service and Friday takeaways with his partner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one's more believable, if I'm honest, because I can already see bits of it happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say nurses aren't going anywhere, because you can't automate a hand on someone's shoulder. Online I'd be the one sharing articles about tech firms making money off the health service. I'd say the government should make hospitals prove an AI tool is safe before it gets near a patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What scares me isn't the AI writing notes. It's management using some staffing program to say a ward of 14 only needs one nurse and two assistants. A computer can count how many patients are on my ward, but it can't tell you which old man is about to pull his drip out at 3am. I'm slow with this stuff, and the ones who are slow get blamed when the system goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push our union branch to demand a say over any staffing software before it goes live, and I'd actually stand for branch rep this time instead of moaning. I'd sit the compulsory training on whatever they bring in, but I'd still keep my paper notes in my tunic pocket. I'd sign every safe-staffing petition going, and I'd write to our local MP, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, mostly, and a bit scared underneath it. I hate feeling stupid in front of a screen, and I know I'd be the one fumbling while the 22-year-olds tap away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the ward would you worry about most in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The healthcare assistants, like Bernie, who's done 25 years and can't type to save her life. If AI does the charts and the managers want "flexible staff", people like her get squeezed out first. Then it's me doing her job and mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep paper notes in your pocket. What happens the first time the ward manager tells you to stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stop in front of her and carry on when she's gone home. That's the honest answer. I know it's not a plan, it's just me being stubborn, and Tom would laugh at me for it.

say: I'd say **nurses** can't be replaced because nobody can automate a hand on a shoulder.
I'd argue online that hospitals must **prove** an AI tool is safe before patients see it.
think: I'm afraid managers will use **staffing software** to justify one nurse for 14 patients.
I'm slow with technology, and **slow staff** get blamed when the system goes wrong.
do: Stand for **branch rep** in the union and demand a say over staffing software.
Sit the **compulsory training** but keep paper notes in his tunic pocket anyway.
Write to the **local MP** about safe staffing for the first time in his life.
feel: **Angry** at management and tech firms, with fear sitting underneath.
**Embarrassed** in advance about fumbling with screens in front of younger nurses.
S1.quote: A computer can count how many patients are on my ward, but it can't tell you which old man is about to pull his drip out at 3am.
fieldNote: His fear is **staffing ratios**, not the note-writing; he trusts managers less than he distrusts machines.
He openly admits the paper notes are **stubbornness**, not a plan, which is unusually honest.
Worry for **Bernie**, a long-serving assistant, shows his loyalty runs to the lowest-paid colleagues.

steps.text: Stand for union branch rep and demand a say on staffing software
Write to the local MP about safe staffing ratios
Keep paper notes in his pocket alongside the tablet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots by 2031. Right. That's the one I'd lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster for patients and that the government let tech companies run the show. I'd be at every protest outside the hospital with a placard, no question. And I'd say it loud enough that the ward manager would probably have a word with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking side of my job, the drug calculations, the handover, the care plans, all of that is gone by 2028, and then managers ask why they're paying a registered nurse to wash and turn people. Then the robots come in 2031 for the washing and turning too. By 2031 I'd be 32, with no savings, in a town with one hospital, watching a machine turn the patients I used to turn. There's nowhere else round here for me to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join every bit of action the union calls, strikes included, even though we can't afford to lose the pay. Tom and I would give up the flat on Mill Street and move somewhere cheaper on the edge of town, maybe a one-bed by the industrial estate. I'd sell the car straight away and put that money aside. And I'd vote for whoever promised to keep nurses on wards by law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor's going. I've always told myself nursing was the safe choice, and in this one it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between the thinking AI and the robots mean for you, in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means three years of being a very expensive pair of hands. The paperwork side of me goes in 2028 and the hands go in 2031, so I'd probably get regraded down to something like a care assistant in between. That's a pay cut while I'm still doing the heavy lifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you avoid new technology. Does two years' warning change that at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, and I know that sounds daft. Two years isn't enough time for someone like me to become a tech person, so I'd rather spend it fighting. If I'm honest, fighting is the only thing I'm any good at outside of nursing.

say: I'd say it's a **disaster** for patients and blame government for letting tech firms decide.
I'd join **protests** outside the hospital even if the ward manager warned him off.
think: The **thinking parts** of nursing go by 2028, leaving managers asking why they pay registered nurses.
By **2031** robots take the hands-on work, and his town has no other hospital.
He expects to be **regraded down** in the three-year gap, losing pay while doing heavy lifting.
do: Join every **union action**, strikes included, even though the household can't afford lost pay.
Give up the **Mill Street flat** for a cheaper one-bed on the edge of town.
Sell the **car** straight away and keep that money as their only cushion.
feel: **Sick**, like the floor is going out from under him.
**Betrayed**, because he chose nursing believing it was the safe job.
S2.quote: By 2031 I'd be 32, with no savings, in a town with one hospital, watching a machine turn the patients I used to turn.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** as a pay cut, not a breathing space.
Two years' warning **doesn't move** him towards technology; he spends it on fighting instead.
He admits fighting is his **only skill** outside nursing, which is both proud and bleak.

steps.text: Join every union strike and protest outside Harlow Bridge hospital
Move from the Mill Street flat to a cheaper one-bed
Sell the car and keep the money as a cushion
Vote for whoever promises to keep nurses on wards by law

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So I'd be 32 at the AGI part and 35 when the robots come. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing as before, just with a bit less panic in my voice. Nurses need to organise now, while there's time, and get safe staffing written into law before 2031. I'd be pushing that line hard on the union page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time to fight, and I'm not leaving nursing because a tech company says so. But I know the merger and the rent don't wait five years. I'd still be skint the whole time, just with a longer countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stand for branch rep and actually do it properly, with monthly meetings in the canteen. I'd try to put 50 a month aside, even if that means no holiday this year. Tom's been on at me to look at district nursing, going into people's homes, because robots would struggle with somebody's cluttered front room. I'd maybe go and shadow a district nurse for a day, but I'm not promising more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, angry, a bit more in control than with two years. It's like knowing a storm's coming next week instead of tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why district nursing, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom's idea. He says a robot can't climb the stairs in a terraced house, find the key under the plant pot and calm down a man who thinks you're the council. He's probably right, but I like my ward and my old ladies, and I don't like change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd save. What would that actually look like in a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifty a month into the pot, which is the cost of our Friday takeaway plus the streaming. No new trainers. And I'd stop lending money to my brother, which is the hardest one, because he always needs it.

say: I'd say nurses must **organise now** and get safe staffing into law before 2031.
I'd push that **message** hard on the union's online page.
think: Five years is **enough time** to fight, and I refuse to quit nursing for a tech firm.
The **merger and rent** still squeeze me now, so I'd be broke through the whole countdown.
do: Run proper **monthly branch meetings** in the canteen as union rep.
Put aside **50 a month** by dropping takeaways, streaming and new trainers.
Shadow a **district nurse** for one day, without promising anything more.
feel: **Uneasy** and angry, but a bit more in control than with two years.
Like knowing a **storm** is coming next week instead of tomorrow.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to fight, and I'm not leaving nursing because a tech company says so.
fieldNote: The extra three years turns his reaction from protest to **organising**, a real shift.
District nursing comes from his partner, not him, and he **resists** even a good idea.
Saving means stopping **loans to his brother**, a family pressure he hadn't mentioned before.

steps.text: Run monthly union branch meetings in the hospital canteen
Save 50 a month by dropping takeaways and streaming
Stop lending money to his brother

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036, and robots in 2039. I'd be nearly 40 by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say ten years is a gift, and the health service has no excuse not to plan properly. I'd say nurses should be in the room when the plans get made, not told afterwards. Same message, but calmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I can't use being scared as an excuse. I'd have to actually learn the stuff I've been dodging. The tablets and the systems, I mean, because otherwise I'd be the dinosaur on the ward. That's the bit that bothers me most, if I'm honest, more than the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd still be fighting the merger and trying to keep nights. In the first few years I'd do the hospital's digital skills course, the one I skipped last spring. I'd keep up the union work and I'd start asking about the district nursing course properly, maybe in year three or four, when I can see where it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the other two, but grumpy. It's the feeling of knowing you've got homework due and you've left it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom the night you decided to do that digital skills course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say "don't laugh". Then I'd ask him to show me how to do the online bits, because he's better with that stuff than me. He'd be unbearable about it for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked about money all through. Does a decade change the money worry at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The decade changes the AI worry, not the money one. I'd still be on a lower band with rent going up every year and nothing in the bank. AI or no AI, I'm one broken boiler away from a bad month.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, and the health service has no excuse not to plan.
I'd insist nurses are **in the room** when the plans get made.
think: A decade removes **fear as an excuse**, so I'd have to learn the systems I avoid.
Becoming the **ward dinosaur** worries me more than the robots themselves.
do: Keep **fighting the merger** and hold on to night shifts for now.
Sign up for the **digital skills course** he skipped last spring.
Ask about the **district nursing course** properly around year three or four.
feel: **Calmer** than with two or five years, but grumpy about it.
Like having **homework** due that he has left too long.
S4.quote: Ten years means I can't use being scared as an excuse. I'd have to actually learn the stuff I've been dodging.
fieldNote: The longest warning is the only one that moves him towards **learning tech**.
He separates the **AI worry** from the money worry, and only the first one eases.
One **broken boiler** from a bad month: his thin cushion keeps him anxious whatever the timeline.

steps.text: Keep fighting the ward merger to hold on to night shifts
Take the hospital's digital skills course he skipped last spring
Ask about the district nursing course around year three

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years, no savings, one hospital, and I'd be regraded down before the robots even turned up. What would help is a law on nurse-to-patient numbers, so no software can decide my ward needs fewer of us, and some kind of public fund to retrain people like me without losing a year's pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who I'd blame. I'd blame the people at the top who'd buy this stuff to save money, not the machines. A robot doesn't decide to cut a ward. A board does. I went into nursing to hold people's hands, not to hold a tablet while a computer tells me how many hands I'm allowed.

headlineQuote: I went into nursing to hold people's hands, not to hold a tablet while a computer tells me how many hands I'm allowed.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old night nurse** on an elderly care ward at the town's only hospital.
He rents a flat with his partner Tom, and the **night allowance** covers their rent.
He distrusts **managers and tech firms** more than machines, and answers every picture by organising through his union.
He moves from anxious to **alarmed** in the two-year picture, expecting to be regraded down before robots arrive.
Only the **ten-year** picture pushes him to learn the systems he has always dodged.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years with no savings and one local hospital leaves him nowhere to go.
whatWouldHelp: A **staffing law** fixing nurse-to-patient numbers so no software can cut his ward.
A **public fund** to retrain nurses without losing a year's pay.
